references.text: Moses' hand became leprous and was then healed when God showed him a sign—an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' power over leprosy.
Miriam was struck with leprosy and then healed after Moses' intercession, demonstrating God's power to remove leprosy.
Naaman was healed of leprosy through the prophet Elisha—a significant Old Testament healing of leprosy that Jesus himself refers to in Luke 4:27.
Matthew's parallel account of the same event where Jesus touches the leper and says, "I will, be clean!" and the man is immediately cleansed.
Mark's parallel account of the healing of the leper, where Jesus stretches out his hand, touches him, and says, "I will, be clean!"
The preceding verse providing context: a man full of leprosy falls down before Jesus and asks for healing with the words, "if you are willing, you can make me clean".

Jesus himself mentions that there were many lepers in Israel during the time of the prophet Elisha, but none of them were cleansed except the Syrian Naaman—a foreshadowing of his own power to cleanse lepers.
Another healing of lepers in the Gospel of Luke: Jesus heals ten leprous men, demonstrating his continued power over this disease.
The prophecy that God will answer before they cry out—Jesus answers immediately and willingly to the leper's prayer, reflecting God's readiness to help.
Jesus as high priest can have compassion on our weaknesses—his touching of the leper shows his willingness to approach the unclean with empathy.
